7.9. store tap innebærer en lite effektiv utnyttelse av sjøarealene

key_figures.quote: Daglig seiler nærmere 1300 fartøyer i norsk innenriksfart.
key_figures.statement: The authors report that nearly 1300 vessels sail in Norwegian domestic waters daily; this is a contextual figure, not a result from a study described in the segment.

key_figures.quote: I juli 2007 ble det etablert trafikkseparasjonssystem på strekningen Vardø–Røst for skip over 5 000 bruttotonn, samt skip som fører farlig og/eller forurensende last.
key_figures.statement: The authors report that in July 2007 a traffic separation scheme was established on the Vardø–Røst stretch for ships over 5 000 gross tonnage and ships carrying dangerous and/or polluting cargo.

key_figures.quote: Restrukturering og omlegging av færøysk akvakulturnæring etter sykdomskrisen med store tap i 2001–2002, har resultert i at generasjonstapet på Færøyene etter dette har ligget på 5–10 %
key_figures.statement: The authors report that Faroese cohort losses after restructuring following the 2001–2002 disease crisis have been 5–10 %.

key_figures.quote: I gjennomsnitt for Norge var tapet i produksjonen på sitt laveste i kalenderåret 2000 med 15 %.
key_figures.statement: The authors report that Norwegian production losses were at their lowest in calendar year 2000, at 15 %.

key_figures.quote: I Skottland var tapet på 2007-generasjonen 28 %, på nivå med våre mest tapsutsatte fylker i 2008, mens i Chile var tapet på 2007-generasjonen 43 %.
key_figures.statement: The authors report losses of 28 % for Scotland’s 2007 generation and 43 % for Chile’s 2007 generation, comparing the former with Norway’s highest-loss counties in 2008.

key_figures.quote: I 2008 utgjorde det norske produksjonstapet av laks og ørret 49,3 millioner fisk.
key_figures.statement: The authors report that Norwegian production losses of salmon and trout totalled 49,3 million fish in 2008.

key_figures.quote: Tapet i form av totalt påløpte produksjonskostnader utgjorde da mer enn 550 millioner kroner i 2008.
key_figures.statement: The authors estimate that total production costs incurred for lost fish in Norway exceeded 550 million kroner in 2008, assuming an average lost fish size of ca. 1 kg.

key_figures.quote: Det potensielle brutto inntektstapet hvis fisken hadde blitt foret frem til vanlig slaktestørrelse er selvsagt vesentlig høyere, anslagsvis 4,9 milliarder kroner.
key_figures.statement: The authors estimate a potential gross revenue loss of 4,9 billion kroner in Norway in 2008 if lost fish had been raised to normal slaughter size.

key_figures.quote: Rundt 85 % av tapet er dødfisk inklusive noe fisk utsortert ved slakting, altså fisk rammet av sykdom eller lidelser.
key_figures.statement: The authors estimate that around 85 % of recorded losses are dead fish, including some fish sorted out at slaughter, indicating fish affected by disease or other conditions.

key_figures.quote: For akvakulturanleggene gjelder et generelt ferdselsforbud 20 meter rundt anleggene medregnet ytre flytebøyer, og et fiskeforbud i en hundremeterssone.
key_figures.statement: The authors describe a general passage prohibition 20 meters around aquaculture facilities, including outer buoys, and a fishing prohibition in a hundred-meter zone.

key_figures.quote: Ytre Hvaler nasjonalpark ble opprettet i 2009 og dekker et totalareal på ca. 354 km2, hvorav 340 km2 er sjøareal.
key_figures.statement: The authors report that Ytre Hvaler National Park, established in 2009, covers ca. 354 km2 in total, including 340 km2 of sea area.

key_figures.quote: I 2001 ble det nedsatt et rådgivende tverrsektorielt utvalg som skulle gi råd om mulige marine områder som kunne inngå i en nasjonal marin verneplan. Utvalget leverte i 2004 en omforent tilråding om beskyttelse/vern av 36 områder
key_figures.statement: The authors report that a cross-sector advisory committee delivered an agreed recommendation in 2004 to protect or conserve 36 marine areas for a national marine conservation plan.

pq_notes.A0: The authors describe coastal space as limited and increasingly contested by aquaculture, shipping, fisheries, recreation, housing, tourism, energy development and conservation. Municipal coastal-zone plans and individual permit decisions are the main arenas for balancing these interests. Since 1.7. 2009, municipalities may distinguish the aquaculture land-use category by species, but whether they will use this power remains uncertain. The authors note that broad multi-use designations have become common and may provide less predictability for aquaculture development because municipalities have made limited explicit choices among uses. Under the Aquaculture Act § 16, the legal reading is that decisions should assess how an area can be used efficiently and in a socially optimal way. Safety of navigation, environmental protection and other uses constrain that assessment.
pq_notes.A1: The authors identify suitable sites, water quality, water contact with other farms, site structure, fish quantity, smolt quality, environmental conditions and distance from other farms as factors affecting development and production outcomes. More exposed sites and larger facilities have become attractive through technological change, but require extensive moorings and can conflict with fishing and navigation. Site availability is also shaped by shipping routes, fishing grounds, conservation areas, recreation and municipal zoning. Permit authorities must weigh applicant need against competing uses, disease-hygiene organization and the public interest. The segment links high production losses to location and area-use structure, but cautions that the knowledge base for explaining mortality remains inadequate. The account is descriptive and does not quantify the independent effects of these factors.
pq_notes.A2: The segment describes two levels of interest balancing: municipal planning under the Planning and Building Act, followed by individual aquaculture permit processing under the Aquaculture Act. Municipal plans establish the framework for available areas; applications then receive a case-specific needs and use assessment. Until 1.1. 2010, Fisheries Directorate regional offices coordinated applications and made first-instance decisions; the counties now conduct ongoing processing. Some increases in fish quantities at existing sites have also required municipal planning processes to accommodate new permits. The authors do not provide average processing times or counts of applications, delays or refusals. They note that conflicts can become apparent only when a specific site and its moorings are proposed, while better mapping and planning can help identify issues earlier.
pq_notes.A3: The segment does not describe formal cumulative-effect assessment methods for aquaculture production. It does, however, identify cumulative and regional concerns that bear on such assessment: total fish quantities in facilities, water contact among farms, environmental conditions, and the possibility that feed and faeces affect fish quality in nearby fishing grounds. The authors argue that production losses may reflect area-use and site structure as well as smolt quality and the amount of fish held. They also distinguish direct physical conflicts from impacts on wild fish across a facility’s ecological influence area. Knowledge is insufficient on whether aquaculture alters wild fish migration and spawning patterns, and the causes of recorded mortality are not adequately explained. Mapping of fishing areas and better coastal plans are presented as useful planning supports, not as a complete cumulative-effects methodology.
pq_notes.A4: The authors discuss economic consequences of production losses and the influence of incentives mainly through proposed regulatory arrangements. In 2008, they report losses of 49,3 million salmon and trout; the lost smolt alone was valued at approximately 400 million kroner, total incurred production costs exceeded 550 million kroner, and potential gross revenue foregone was estimated at 4,9 billion kroner. They state that each percentage-point reduction in production loss represents a net cost reduction of 25 million kroner and potential gross first-hand additional revenue of over 200 million kroner. These are authors’ estimates, not independently tested results in this segment. The committee argues that permanent, predictable measures for relocation or reducing regional biomass could encourage loss reduction. The segment also notes possible municipal disappointment about limited local income or economic spillovers, but does not set out a detailed distributional analysis across stakeholders.
pq_notes.A5: The evidence base described includes operating-data registration at food-fish and smolt sites, good records for listed infectious diseases, company-level mortality tracking, Fisheries Directorate maps of fishing interests, shipping-route databases and registered cultural heritage sites. However, the authors say information on other health conditions is inadequate and that industry and regulators lack a suitable tool to analyse and explain recorded losses. A broader fish-health monitoring system, MFISK, began development in 2006 with the Food Safety Authority, the Veterinary Institute and others, but was not completed because industry data were difficult to collect. The authors also identify insufficient knowledge about effects on wild fish behaviour and migration. Digital fairway maps in KYSTINFO and mapping of fishing and recreation areas can inform planning, while technological development has enabled larger, flexible facilities farther offshore. The segment gives no assessment of emerging monitoring technologies beyond these examples.
pq_notes.A6: The authors describe conflicts between aquaculture and shipping, fisheries, recreation, tourism, conservation, cultural heritage and other coastal uses. Fisheries conflicts include competition for fishing grounds and possible ecological effects: the Ryfylke “seisaken” concerns wild saithe feeding on spilled feed near salmon farms, with reported quality and income losses for fishers. The authors say more knowledge is needed on effects on wild fish migration and spawning, while genetic effects of cod farming near spawning grounds are described as well documented. Recreation conflicts include visual impacts, restricted passage and concerns from nearby homes and holiday houses; the segment cites a 2002 conflict mapping that characterized some conflicts as modest to moderate. Legitimate and predictable decisions are supported, in the authors’ account, by identifying interests in plans, mapping fishing and recreation areas, using fairway standards and making decisions proportionate to conservation purposes. They note that local compromises may be difficult, particularly between outside property owners and local businesses.
pq_notes.A7: The authors’ central industry-facing measure is reducing production losses, which they regard as important for both economic and ecological sustainability and efficient use of sea areas. They identify better operating routines and preparedness as relevant at individual companies, alongside attention to smolt quality and transport practices, including fish quantity per transport and transport duration. The segment says that location, water quality, site structure, fish quantities and water contact with other farms likely contribute to differences in losses, but acknowledges that causal knowledge is weak. It further argues that relocation or, where necessary, reducing aggregate biomass in regions with persistent high losses may be needed, supported by permanent and predictable instruments. The committee refers to a proposal elsewhere in the document for regional adjustment of MTB and environmentally motivated relocation. This segment does not detail a complete operational standard or quantify the expected effect of these measures.
pq_notes.A8: The authors identify water contact between farms as a likely important underlying factor in differences in production losses. Location and water quality are also highlighted, and the segment links site structure and the total quantity of fish in facilities to loss outcomes. It suggests that more robust location structures may help explain lower losses in Nordland and the Trøndelag counties compared with counties farther south, while later development in Troms and Finnmark was more directed and drew on experience elsewhere. These are proposed explanations rather than demonstrated causal estimates. The authors emphasize that recorded mortality after sea transfer is poorly explained and that the MFISK monitoring system, intended to improve knowledge of disease and fish health, was not completed because of difficulties obtaining industry data. The segment does not provide specific water-connectivity distances, transmission rates or biosecurity protocols.

segments.summary:
This segment moves from production losses in aquaculture to competing uses of coastal space. It says that monitoring covers operating data and listed infectious diseases, but information on other health conditions and causes of mortality remains weak. The MFISK monitoring initiative, begun in 2006, was not completed because of difficulties collecting industry data. The authors identify smolt quality, site structure, fish quantities, water quality and water contact between farms as likely drivers of losses, while stressing that these explanations are not fully established. They compare national production losses, estimate their economic costs, and argue that reducing losses would improve both economic performance and the efficiency and sustainability of sea-area use. They propose predictable measures that could support relocation or lower biomass in regions with persistently high losses.

The following sections describe coastal-area conflicts involving shipping, fisheries, recreation, tourism, aquaculture types, conservation and cultural heritage. Planning and individual permit decisions are presented as the main settings for balancing these uses. Municipalities gained authority from 1.7. 2009 to differentiate aquaculture areas by species, although broad multi-use zoning remains common and may offer limited certainty to applicants. The authors discuss fairway standards and routing measures, mapped fisheries and recreation interests, protected areas, and the need for better knowledge of effects on wild fish. They distinguish direct spatial conflicts from ecological effects that extend beyond facility boundaries. The segment is a policy and evidence review, with some cited studies and legal frameworks; it repeatedly notes limits in causal knowledge and does not provide a systematic assessment of cumulative effects or application delays.

headings: 9. Plan- og søknadsprosesser knyttet til etablering og flytting av akvakulturanlegg

key_figures.quote: I løpet av programperioden 2007–2010 ble utvalgte marine naturtyper i omtrent halvparten av Norges kystkommuner ferdig kartlagt.
key_figures.statement: The authors report that during the 2007–2010 program period, selected marine habitat types were mapped in approximately half of Norway’s coastal municipalities.

key_figures.quote: Når kartleggingen av marine naturtyper i Hordaland er gjennomført, vil 48,6 % av Norges kystkommuner være ferdig kartlagt.
key_figures.statement: The authors report that completion of the marine habitat mapping in Hordaland would bring the share of Norway’s coastal municipalities mapped to 48,6 %.

key_figures.quote: I områdene utenfor 4 nm fra grunnlinjene er det igangsatt et systematisk bunnkartleggingsprogram (MAREANO-programmet).
key_figures.statement: The authors state that systematic seabed mapping under MAREANO had been initiated in areas outside 4 nm from the baselines.

key_figures.quote: I oktober 2010 la en direktoratsgruppe nedsatt av Olje- og energidepartementet fram en rapport som vurderte femten områder som særlig aktuelle for videre utredning med tanke på etablering av havvindmølleparker i norske farvann.
key_figures.statement: The authors report that in October 2010 a directorate group assessed femten areas in Norwegian waters as particularly relevant for further investigation for offshore wind farms.

key_figures.quote: Åtte av disse områdene, der vindmøllene er tenkt som bunnfaste installasjoner, ligger helt eller delvis innenfor grunnlinjen.
key_figures.statement: The authors report that eight of the wind-farm investigation areas, where turbines were envisaged as fixed-bottom installations, lay wholly or partly inside the baselines.

key_figures.quote: Ved årsskiftet hadde 97 % av alle kystkommunene kystsoneplaner ferdig eller under arbeid.
key_figures.statement: The authors report that at the year-end, 97 % of coastal municipalities had coastal-zone plans completed or in progress.

key_figures.quote: For nye akvakulturanlegg klarert for minst 3600 tonn fisk i sjøen til enhver tid, har det siden 1997 vært adgang til å kreve utarbeidelse av konsekvensutredning.
key_figures.statement: The authors state that since 1997, an impact assessment could be required for new aquaculture facilities authorized for at least 3600 tonnes of fish in the sea at any time.

key_figures.quote: Dersom den omsøkte lokaliseringen faller inn under kriteriene som er listet opp i forskriftens § 4 kan pålegg om konsekvensutredning gis for etablering av større akvakulturanlegg, og for settefiskanlegg for mer enn 5 millioner fisk.
key_figures.statement: The authors explain that under the regulation’s criteria, an impact assessment could be required for larger aquaculture facilities and hatcheries for more than 5 millioner fish.

key_figures.quote: • Komplett søknad videresendes lokaliseringskommunen innen 2 uker.
key_figures.statement: The process timetable states that the county authority forwards a complete application to the municipality where the site is located within 2 weeks.

key_figures.quote: • I samarbeid med kommunen, legger søker søknaden ut til offentlig utlegging i 4 uker.
key_figures.statement: The process timetable states that the applicant, in cooperation with the municipality, makes the application available for public inspection for 4 weeks.

key_figures.quote: • Skal fatte vedtak og /eller avgi uttalelse i løpet av 4 uker fra mottagelse av merknader fra offentlig utlegging og eventuell kommunal uttalelse.
key_figures.statement: The process timetable states that the relevant sector authorities should decide and/or provide comments within 4 weeks after receiving public comments and any municipal statement.

pq_notes.A0: The authors describe spatial decisions as dependent on mapped natural values, site conditions, municipal plans, sector rules, and competing interests. Municipal coastal-zone plans are legally binding and are the main local instrument for enabling aquaculture, while licenses cannot be granted contrary to applicable plans or protection measures. Planning is intended to reconcile interests through open participation and impact analysis. The segment also argues that municipalities’ incentives to make room for aquaculture vary: some see little local economic benefit relative to costs, and may not prioritize plan revision. Regional and intermunicipal planning are presented as options where municipal boundaries impede coordination.
pq_notes.A1: The authors identify site capacity and suitability, existing plan design, environmental and biodiversity knowledge, disease concerns, and changing technology and facility size as factors shaping development opportunities. Some municipalities report that all designated aquaculture areas are occupied; others have unused areas that do not meet current spatial requirements. The segment argues that growth and relocation northward may require revisions to coastal-zone plans and productive relationships with host municipalities. Licensing also depends on municipal plan conformity and sector authorities’ decisions, especially environmental acceptability and balancing area interests. Mapping of habitats and seabeds is presented as important to improving the information available for planning, although coastal mapping is described as costly.
pq_notes.A2: The authors describe a coordinated application route: the applicant submits a complete application to the county authority, which forwards it to the municipality and relevant state sector authorities. The application is publicly announced and inspected; the municipality comments on plans and local interests, while sector authorities decide under their own legislation or provide statements. A refusal by any state sector authority requires the county authority to refuse the application. The timetable shown gives 2 weeks for forwarding to the municipality, 4 weeks for public inspection, and 4 weeks for sector-authority decisions or comments after receiving relevant input. The authors say refusals most often follow Food Safety Authority assessments, while complaints against granted sites are frequent and can lengthen processing; many such issues could have been settled during planning.
pq_notes.A3: The segment discusses impact assessment requirements rather than methods for cumulative-effect assessment. The authors state that municipal land-use plans always require impact assessment and that individual aquaculture projects are a category for which assessment may be required depending on regulatory criteria and site circumstances. A project authorized for at least 3600 tonnes of biomass is treated as a larger facility in this context; hatcheries for more than 5 million fish may also be covered. The assessment is intended to accompany the application through sector-authority review and strengthen the decision basis. The authors note that few project assessments had been prepared, anticipate more as facilities grow and move offshore, and warn that inconsistent regional practice and assessment costs may affect relocation decisions.
pq_notes.A5: The authors identify a short planning history for marine areas and gaps in knowledge of local topography, water quality, currents, biodiversity, recreation, and tourism. They report that mapping programs and online map-based tools are improving data access across sectors. Coastal habitat mapping records findings in the Nature Base; MAREANO uses multibeam mapping, interpretation of acoustic signals, and observation points with video and sampling to document seabed, fauna, and contaminants. The authors argue that extending MAREANO-style mapping to the coast would be costly and suggest seabed-type maps based on multibeam measurements as a possible supplement. They also identify shortages of municipal planning expertise and guidance, particularly in northern and remote municipalities.
pq_notes.A6: The authors identify potential conflicts with fisheries, recreation and holiday homes, biodiversity protection, Sámi interests, offshore wind, cables, pipelines, and other uses. They expect limited conflict between aquaculture and many energy or infrastructure uses, partly because of depth and exposure, and say planning processes can identify and address such interests before development. Participation and influence are uneven: organized groups, residents, and interests represented by public agencies may have different access to information and decision-makers. For northern relocation, the authors emphasize Sámi rights and consultation. They report that complaints against site approvals are numerous and often come from recreational interests, while refusals most often arise from Food Safety Authority assessments; many disputes could have been resolved in plans.
pq_notes.A8: The segment links disease management to spatial planning by noting that the Food Safety Authority administers disease-control zones, which may cross municipal, county, or directorate-region boundaries. It also says that emerging disease issues contribute to the need to revise coastal plans. However, it provides no analysis of water connectivity between farms, transmission pathways, or operational biosecurity measures, so those aspects cannot be assessed from this segment.

segments.summary:
This segment first covers mapping of marine biodiversity and seabed conditions. The national mapping program surveyed selected marine habitats and key areas for species and fish stocks; during 2007–2010, selected habitats were mapped in approximately half of Norway’s coastal municipalities. When mapping in Hordaland was complete, the stated coverage would be 48,6 %. The MAREANO program maps seabed areas outside 4 nm from the baselines using multibeam sonar, interpretation of acoustic data, and video and physical sampling. The authors argue that similar coastal mapping would be costly, but that seabed-type maps could complement habitat surveys and support municipal planning.

Section 8.7 considers potential conflicts with offshore wind, wave power, cables, pipelines, seismic surveys, and other uses. The authors expect limited aquaculture conflict with many of these uses, while noting that planning processes should identify and reconcile competing interests. The segment then outlines Norway’s planning framework and aquaculture application process. Municipal coastal-zone plans are central and legally binding; the authors report that 97 % of coastal municipalities had plans completed or underway at year-end. Impact assessments may be required for larger facilities, including those authorized for at least 3600 tonnes of fish at any time, and hatcheries for more than 5 million fish.

The authors identify outdated plans, varying municipal incentives and expertise, incomplete environmental knowledge, and uneven participation as planning challenges. Applications involve municipal public review and decisions by sector authorities; refusals most often follow Food Safety Authority assessments, and complaints can prolong processing. The segment notes disease-control zones that cross administrative boundaries. It provides no detailed method or result for cumulative-effect assessment, and its proposed expansion of coastal mapping is a recommendation rather than a completed survey.

key_figures.statement: The committee proposes starting from the 23 coastal areas used in 2009 to assess suitable areas for new permits; this is a policy proposal referring to an earlier administrative division.

pq_notes.A0: The authors’ proposals connect spatial development to current conditions, seabed and habitat mapping, and disease-conscious zoning. A national current catalogue could inform production-area and stocking-zone boundaries and help assess locations for individual farms or clusters. The committee proposes production areas divided into stocking zones, with coordinated stocking, fallowing and disease control. It argues that these scientific boundaries should guide where aquaculture can be assessed, while municipal plans and other coastal uses remain in force and may constrain available sites. A two-stage process is proposed: regulations establish areas and zones using professional criteria, while municipal planning allocates sites and weighs competing interests. The segment emphasizes that regional and intermunicipal planning cooperation is needed.
pq_notes.A1: The authors identify site opportunity as dependent on current patterns, hydrology, topography, seabed substrate, habitats, exposure and wind, alongside disease transmission and operational needs. They argue that existing coastal maps and observations are insufficient, and propose a national current catalogue and improved mapping. Their zoning proposal links site availability to disease-safe separation, coordinated production cycles and fallowing. Existing administrative boundaries may not match natural marine boundaries, so the committee recommends boundaries based on scientific criteria instead. Municipal plans, national salmon fjords and shipping lanes continue to constrain site choice. The segment describes the licensing framework only in relation to ongoing site applications and proposed changes to coordination; it does not comprehensively assess the licensing system.
pq_notes.A2: The segment does not give a general account of the ordinary application process or report application-processing durations or rejection rates. It says current practice is that the first applicant receives permission when the applicant’s need is justified, the site is suitable and other requirements are met. The committee recommends retaining that practice but holding joint meetings of the relevant authorities for cases within each production area, so applications can be considered against the planned spatial structure. It rejects processing applications in batches, such as twice a year, as potentially reducing industry flexibility and creating administrative burdens. For creating production areas and stocking zones, it proposes a two-stage regulatory process, with regional and local input, followed by municipal planning to allocate sites. It notes that these processes will be time-consuming and that conflicts may emerge around existing sites and prospective development areas.
pq_notes.A3: The segment does not describe cumulative-effect assessment methods or their use in decisions about production volumes. It does propose that environmental sustainability indicators be developed and related to conditions within each production area, where they could guide possible production scale. The authors argue that current models can describe spatial and temporal differences but may struggle with absolute levels, and that continuous validation against observations is important. Model grid resolution also limits representation of fine-scale fjord currents and farm details. A national current catalogue, linked to observations and existing fjord models, is presented as a tool for planning and site selection. The passage identifies uncertainty and limits in model performance but does not set out a cumulative-impact assessment framework.
pq_notes.A4: The segment does not discuss economic instruments such as area fees or taxes. It does consider distributional and operational consequences of the proposed zoning system. The committee expects transition costs for affected operators, particularly small producers facing greater separation between disease-distinct sites and constraints on harvest timing from coordinated fallowing. It argues that smaller operators may need to cooperate or share operations to maintain seasonal stocking patterns, while larger firms may more readily support infrastructure across dispersed sites. The committee sees a trade-off between growth or maximum sustainable production and facilitating small-scale production. It expects public authorities to face substantial costs during implementation, with ongoing administration later expected to be around the current level. It also anticipates possible longer-term industry growth and employment in some districts, but says effects will take time.
pq_notes.A5: The authors identify numerical fjord models, field observations of currents, salinity and temperature, and maps of topography, substrate and habitats as key parts of the evidence base. They propose a national current catalogue covering the coast and relevant fjords, coordinated by the Institute of Marine Research and made available through standardized formats. NorKyst-800, developed by the Institute of Marine Research, the Meteorological Institute and NIVA, is described as a potential coast-wide foundation and boundary condition for finer fjord models. The committee stresses continuous model validation and cautions that models may represent spatial and temporal differences better than absolute levels. It also proposes extending Mareano mapping toward coastal waters and making data collected by other actors accessible. The segment identifies mapping and model limitations but does not assess emerging technologies beyond these tools.
pq_notes.A6: The authors identify potential conflicts between aquaculture, existing farm locations, future development interests, municipal land-use plans, shipping, fisheries and other coastal interests. They distinguish the scientific task of defining production areas and disease-safe zones from the democratic planning process that allocates sites and weighs competing uses. Natural boundaries should take precedence over administrative borders, which may cross areas and zones. To make conflicts manageable, the committee proposes first drawing ideal zones using scientific criteria without accounting for existing sites, then overlaying existing locations to identify practical clashes and cases that may require relocation. It invites industry proposals for zone boundaries if they are unanimous and within clear parameters. The authors argue that involving industry and using transparent, bounded processes can support workable solutions, but also recognize that the transition is challenging and resource-intensive.
pq_notes.A7: The committee encourages industry to contribute existing hydrological observations collected at farms, which are currently used internally, to improve model validation and the shared current catalogue. It proposes investigating whether data-sharing should be voluntary or required, including the costs of any requirement. For production areas and stocking zones, it invites operators to devise unanimous zone arrangements within clearly defined limits. The authors expect close industry participation to help identify and voluntarily resolve poorly located farms and infectious bridges before authorities resort to compulsory relocation. They also point to shared operations and co-location as ways smaller operators could meet the demands of coordinated stocking across zones. These are proposals and expectations, not reported evaluations of measures already implemented.
pq_notes.A8: Biosecurity is central to the proposed production-area system. The committee argues that areas separated by disease-prevention barriers should coordinate stocking, fallowing and disease control in two-year cycles. It proposes dividing each production area into at least four stocking zones and strengthening fallowing by requiring simultaneous fallowing of all sites in a zone for at least one month within the existing post-harvest fallowing period. Production-area boundaries and zone design should account for current-driven water contact, with current modelling helping identify infectious links between farms or groups. The authors distinguish the relatively longer persistence of sea lice in open water from viruses and bacteria, and explain that fallowing alone may be insufficient against lice where zones would need to be impractically large. They therefore present zoning and fallowing as one of several interacting control measures.

segments.summary:
This segment presents proposals for improving the evidence and spatial organization underpinning sustainable aquaculture. The committee recommends a national current catalogue to support production-area boundaries, stocking zones and farm siting. Numerical models provide three-dimensional time series, but their grid cells, from 100 m to 1 km along their edges, cannot capture the finest local details; models also require continuous validation and may represent spatial and temporal variation better than absolute levels. NorKyst-800, with 800 meters grid resolution, was scheduled to be operational and quality-assured during 2011 and could support finer fjord models with resolutions from 100 to 200 m. Establishing the catalogue was estimated at Ca. 10 millioner kr. The committee also proposes better coastal mapping and investigating whether operators should share hydrological observations already collected at many farms.

The segment’s central management proposal is to divide the coast into production areas and stocking zones, coordinate stocking and disease control, and align fallowing. It proposes four stocking zones per production area and simultaneous fallowing across a zone for at least one month within the existing minimum two-month post-harvest fallowing period. The committee suggests starting from the 23 areas used in a 2009 assessment, while emphasizing that final boundaries should reflect natural and disease-related conditions rather than administrative borders. It recognizes trade-offs for small operators, who may need to cooperate, and proposes a staged process: establish areas and zones through regulations, then use municipal planning to allocate sites and balance competing interests. Industry participation, shared data and voluntary relocations are encouraged, with compulsory relocation proposed as a backstop. The segment describes recommendations and anticipated consequences, not results of an evaluation of their implementation.

key_figures.statement: The authors describe the 2004 regulation as limiting each aquaculture licence to at most four sites.

pq_notes.A0: The authors propose managing production through predefined, predictable action rules, including regional biomass adjustments based on production losses and environmental relocation of licences. They argue that production areas and coordinated fallowing and stocking zones can support sustainable area use and collective disease management. Site suitability and area capacity should be considered at a broader scale than the individual site. Environmental indicators, including losses, sea-lice pressure and escaped-fish impacts, are intended to guide decisions; the authors do not specify the proposed loss thresholds a and b. They argue that sustainability and efficient area use should take precedence over district-policy considerations when deciding where licences are located.
pq_notes.A1: The authors identify site availability and the structure of locations as important constraints on development. They propose that operators in areas with high losses may move licences to areas with lower losses, provided they obtain sites cleared for the additional biomass. Coordinated stocking and fallowing zones are intended to improve health and environmental conditions, while crisis sites could provide temporary alternatives when ordinary sites cannot be used. Operators with fewer licences may face particular difficulty adapting to zone-based operations; shared operation and co-location are identified as tools for smaller businesses. The authors also argue that regional loss-based biomass rules should apply collectively, although they acknowledge that larger operators with activity across several regions may benefit more from relocation opportunities.
pq_notes.A2: This segment does not describe the full application process or report typical processing times, rejection rates or stages where delays most often occur. It does propose that, when production areas or stocking zones are established, applications from operators who must move may receive priority over other applicants for a limited, necessary period. Authorities should assess each applicant’s need for the site concretely, and ordinary applications should not be delayed longer than necessary. After that period, applications are handled normally, with no guaranteed preferential treatment beyond the assessment of need against competing applications. The proposal could affect statutory processing deadlines and is suggested for the salmon-licensing regulation.
pq_notes.A3: The authors propose using production areas as the regional unit for calculating losses and adjusting permitted biomass, and stocking zones for coordinated stocking and fallowing. This is a proposed cumulative, area-level approach rather than reliance on individual-site assessments alone. For sea lice, they propose developing an operational indicator from ongoing research and tracking total adult female lice at site, stocking-zone and production-area scales. They identify knowledge challenges in measuring lice on wild and farmed fish, accounting for biomass, and monitoring resistance. Loss data are considered adequate to begin applying the proposed rule, but the authors call for better quality assurance, controls and fish-counting methods. They caution that loss is not a complete sustainability indicator and that lice and escaped-fish indicators should supplement it.
pq_notes.A4: The authors reject a proposal to make the industry’s relocation costs subject to specific cost-sharing rules, arguing that the industry should bear costs associated with achieving sustainable operations and growth. They would instead make early voluntary movers more attractive relocation opportunities than operators who must be ordered to move. Regional biomass reductions could reduce affected operators’ short-term earnings, while lower losses and more efficient area use are expected to benefit the industry over the longer term. They anticipate that relocation could shift employment and activity from areas that lose production to receiving areas, including increased activity in the north at the expense of western Norway. Larger operators may gain most directly from relocation, although remaining operators may benefit from more space and lower total biomass.
pq_notes.A5: The authors draw on monthly biomass reporting, existing site and loss statistics, legal provisions, and ongoing research on lice monitoring and fish counts. They say production loss data can be improved by calculating losses over a full production generation rather than using the current model, which they consider misleadingly low. They recommend reporting the origin of stocked fish to support risk-based supervision and tracing escaped fish. Data quality is a central caveat: reporting accuracy and controls need to improve, and the authors expect active use of data to strengthen quality. A working group and the Exactus project were expected to improve knowledge of fish counting and biomass measurement. Better counting equipment, methods and routines could also improve escape statistics.
pq_notes.A6: The authors identify potential conflicts between operators competing for the same sites, between existing operators and applicants seeking nearby sites, and between relocation priorities and ordinary applications. They argue that a nearby application should not be rejected solely because an existing operator objects that the sites are close, where the concern is not a substantive transmission risk; they call for revision of the Food Safety Authority’s guidance. They also acknowledge fairness concerns when all operators in a high-loss production area face biomass reductions, including operators whose own losses are low. Their rationale is collective sustainability and shared benefits. Predictability, broad acceptance of rules, transparent data and timely information are presented as conditions for legitimate implementation.
pq_notes.A7: The authors say industry can improve area efficiency through voluntary relocation, co-location, shared operation and collective coordination of stocking, fallowing and disease-control measures. They consider shared operation especially useful for smaller actors who may struggle to operate across multiple stocking zones. Operators are expected to identify and apply for additional nearby sites themselves when grouping sites can improve use of regional production capacity. The authors recommend that the industry improve fish counting and reporting, quality assurance, and the quality and size of stocked smolts to reduce losses. They also suggest that an industry organization could apply for suitable crisis sites and establish clear rules for their temporary use.
pq_notes.A8: Biosecurity and waterborne disease transmission are central to the proposed use of production areas and stocking zones. The authors argue that coordinated stocking and fallowing, area-wide treatment coordination and suitable site groupings can improve fish health and reduce infection spread. They note that neighbouring sites may be considered a group when they are not epidemiologically separate; they do not regard proximity alone as grounds to reject a site application, except where the complaint concerns transmission to or from the facility. Crisis sites could allow a new stocking at another site in the same zone after disease-control measures make an ordinary site unusable. The authors also propose reporting the source of stocked fish, the stocking date and the wellboat used, to support risk-based supervision and disease investigation.

segments.summary:
This segment presents proposals for restructuring aquaculture site use and managing production at regional scale. The authors suggest temporary priority in site applications for operators who must relocate, while requiring authorities to assess site needs individually and limit delays to what relocation requires. They discuss phasing out or reducing production at less suitable sites, use of co-location and shared operation, and temporary crisis sites for emergencies such as disease outbreaks. They also propose repealing the four-to-six rule; registered marine sites for salmon and rainbow trout food-fish licences had fallen from over 1800 to 1023 by 31 December 2010.

The main proposal is a regional action rule that adjusts permitted biomass according to average production losses over the two preceding generations, alongside permission to move licences from high-loss to lower-loss production areas. The authors give illustrative benchmarks: average losses of 10–15 % may be acceptable, while over 20–25 % is concerning. They suggest annual downward adjustments of 2–5 % and upward adjustments of 5–10 %, but leave the actual thresholds for political decision. They argue that loss data are usable to start the system, while requiring better quality control and monitoring. Production loss is not a complete sustainability measure; sea lice and escaped fish should also inform decisions.

The segment further recommends better lice indicators and reporting at site, stocking-zone and production-area scales, and reporting the origin of stocked fish. Its proposals are policy and regulatory recommendations, not evaluations of implemented measures. It identifies unresolved legal questions, data-quality limitations and possible distributional effects, including shifts in employment and production between regions.

pq_notes.A0: The authors argue that sustainable aquaculture requires a new, sustainable site structure and predictable, integrated planning. They recommend state expectations for regional and municipal plans, while retaining local room for decision-making. They also recommend no further growth through new licences or general increases in maximum permitted biomass until production areas are established and measures can be implemented. Closed sea-based systems and land-based production could create additional siting options, but do not remove environmental constraints, including nutrient-discharge limits.
pq_notes.A1: The authors identify environmental capacity, site structure, fish health, disease transmission and availability of smolts as factors affecting development. They propose production areas divided into smolt-release zones, partly to establish areas separated for biosecurity. Transport between areas is a disease risk and can harm smolt health and welfare; the ideal, in their view, is for each production area to be self-sufficient in smolts. Larger smolts and shorter marine production time could improve survival and area efficiency, but may require greater hatchery capacity. Closed systems may enable production at some sites constrained for open cages, subject to discharge, health and welfare requirements.
pq_notes.A2: The segment does not describe the complete coastal-site application process. It does identify processing of applications for establishing or expanding smolt facilities under the Water Resources Act as a bottleneck: these cases are outside the regulation setting processing deadlines for site-clearance applications. The authors recommend reviewing this processing to find efficiencies, while noting that hydrological measurements and other case-specific features make faster decisions challenging. They provide no quantified processing times or rejection rates and state that they lack information to assess the proposal's economic and administrative consequences.
pq_notes.A3: The authors find current seabed sampling inadequate for assessing cumulative effects of very large farms and farm groups. They propose allowing authorities to require monitoring under NS-EN ISO 16665:2005, with sampling locations selected for local current and depth conditions and more samples to improve representativeness. Existing C-surveys, with set locations and numbers of samples, may not adequately cover large sites or clusters, especially in fjords. The authors also identify a methodological gap: there is no suitable method for monitoring organic impacts on deep hard seabed and slopes, and recommend prioritising its development.
pq_notes.A4: The authors describe a proposed allocation of costs and obligations across producers. For grouped-site monitoring, costs should be shared among operators according to the biomass cleared at each site, not the fish present when samples are taken. For escaped-fish removal, all aquaculture operators in a production area would bear objective shared responsibility, even where an individual escape cannot be attributed to them; operators could seek reimbursement if a source is established. The segment also discusses a possible industry-funded fund to cover part of farmers' insurance deductibles following compulsory slaughter, but does not present it as an established instrument.
pq_notes.A5: The authors identify a need for better monitoring methods and data systems. They propose organising total adult female sea-lice counts at site, smolt-release-zone and production-area levels as an initial basis for a future indicator and action rule. They also recommend developing monitoring for impacts on hard seabed. Closed sea-based and land-based systems could enable innovation and production in new areas, with potential environmental benefits if effluent is treated, but they require more energy and present fish-health and welfare risks. The authors state that new methods must be tested and documented as welfare-safe before use.
pq_notes.A6: The authors describe tensions between production growth and the time and capacity required to implement sustainability measures. They recommend pausing new licences and general maximum-biomass increases until production areas and a sustainable site structure are established. They also propose cross-municipal and cross-county planning and coordinated state expectations to improve predictability, while keeping those expectations broad enough to preserve local discretion. Shared action on disease, sea lice and escaped fish is presented as a way for operators to meet obligations efficiently and demonstrate social responsibility. The segment does not report specific planning disputes with other coastal users.
pq_notes.A7: The authors recommend that operators establish permanent cooperative arrangements within each production area. Possible tasks include coordinating fallowing and disease or sea-lice control, planning emergency slaughter, sharing relevant data, and removing escaped fish from rivers. A national coordinating structure could support information exchange, competence and development. They also recommend more offensive coordinated fallowing to reduce sea-lice pressure on migrating salmon smolts, while cautioning that it would not provide the same benefit for sea trout and Arctic char that remain in fjords and coastal waters year-round.
pq_notes.A8: The authors treat connectivity between farms and areas as a biosecurity issue. They propose production areas divided into smolt-release zones to create areas separated for disease control, and describe fish transport between areas as a source of infection risk and potential harm to smolt health and welfare. They argue that local smolt supply could reduce long-distance transport and that each production area should ideally be self-sufficient. Coordinated fallowing and joint disease control are among the proposed industry tasks. The segment does not quantify waterborne transmission distances or specify hydrodynamic thresholds.

segments.summary: This segment presents recommendations on sustainability rules, technology, environmental monitoring, planning and cooperation. For sea lice, the authors propose organising counts of adult female lice by site, smolt-release zone and production area as a basis for a future indicator and tiered action rule. Measures could include additional treatments and coordinated fallowing; the authors stress that fallowing must match the timing and extent of smolt migration, and will not benefit sea trout and Arctic char in the same way as migrating salmon smolts. For escaped salmon, they propose an indicator of genetic effects in designated rivers and a requirement for zero first-generation farmed fish during spawning once a threshold is exceeded. Industry-wide responsibility within production areas would fund removal, with fin clipping discussed as a practical identification method. The authors note unresolved legal questions about authority to impose shared duties under the Aquaculture Act. They recommend no new licences or general biomass increases before production areas are established, while proposing easier establishment of closed sea-based and land-based production to encourage technology development. These systems could offer new siting options but have energy, discharge, fish-health and welfare constraints. Monitoring recommendations include improved sampling beneath large cages, cumulative-effects surveys using NS-EN ISO 16665:2005, and development of a method for hard seabeds. The largest cages are reported to exceed 50 meters in diameter; estimated B-survey costs are kr 15 000 to 20 000 and C-survey costs kr 50 000 to 130 000. The authors also recommend more efficient processing of smolt-facility applications, state expectations for planning, and permanent industry cooperation. The segment mainly presents proposals and identifies knowledge gaps, rather than reporting evaluated outcomes.

pq_notes.A0: The authors argue that comprehensive regional and municipal coastal plans are a prerequisite for sustainable aquaculture development. The 2009 Planning and Building Act changes, high current utilisation in some areas, growth opportunities elsewhere, larger facilities, co-location, joint operations and emergency sites all create a need to revise and coordinate spatial plans. They recommend pilots spanning different growth, restructuring and local-opinion contexts, with state-sector participation and attention to conservation and Water Framework Directive plans. The authors also recommend evaluating the property-tax arrangement after production areas and release zones are established, rather than assessing an area fee in this report.
pq_notes.A1: The authors identify limited site availability as a central constraint: suitable aquaculture sites are a scarce resource. Development prospects also depend on planning competence, whether coastal plans are up to date, local growth or restructuring needs, and the presence of local support or opposition. Larger facilities, co-location, joint operations and the need for emergency sites increase planning demands. The segment does not analyse licensing rules or fish-health constraints in detail. Its proposals are to improve planning through regional and intermunicipal pilot projects and a shared guidance document, and to evaluate municipal property taxation once production areas and release zones are established.
pq_notes.A3: This segment does not describe cumulative-effects assessment methods or how production-level assessments are formally embedded in site decisions. The authors do call for regional monitoring robust enough to document sustainable operations at regional scale, noting that the Water Framework Directive requires a fine-grained monitoring network. They argue that baseline ecological information is lacking for assessing aquaculture effects on fish populations, fisheries and fjord environments. The proposed before-and-after study in inner Ofotfjorden is presented as an unusual opportunity to examine ecological effects, but it is described as a proposed project, not completed evidence. The authors also recommend that planning pilots identify supplementary knowledge needs and that a guide catalogue relevant maps and data.
pq_notes.A4: The authors apply the economic principle that pricing scarce goods can encourage more socially efficient resource use, and consider payment for exclusive use of scarce sea space reasonable. They report that municipalities gained authority from 1.1.2009 to levy property tax on floating marine aquaculture facilities, based on the value of cages and equipment. The reported tax is between ca. 25 000 and 70 000 kr per site per year; the authors describe these sums as modest in aquaculture terms. They agree that an annual area fee accruing to municipalities could strengthen local ties weakened by industry restructuring and concentration of slaughtering. They do not reassess an area fee, but recommend evaluating the existing tax after production areas and release zones are established.
pq_notes.A5: The authors propose a planning guide that would improve competence and direct users to maps and data on currents, wave heights and depths, as well as information on fisheries, shipping, conservation, wild-fish migration routes, recreation, landscape and other public interests. They identify research needs including indicators for escaped fish and sea lice, effects on wild fish, environmental monitoring, closed systems, disease and parasite prevention and treatment, feed, sterile fish, environmental effects, fish welfare and aquaculture technology. They describe a proposed before-and-after ecological study in inner Ofotfjorden, with four work packages, as a rare research opportunity; it had not yet been carried out. They also call for more professionalised innovation, with more research in established research infrastructure and less in operational production.
pq_notes.A6: The authors say pilot plans should include places with local engagement in aquaculture and places with local opposition, so that different planning challenges and methods can be tested. They recommend full, open planning processes with participation and coordination, especially involving state-sector agencies, and dissemination of lessons to other regions and national authorities. The guide should address objection procedures, agency roles, engagement with industry, organisations and the public, and ways to map aquaculture potential. The authors expect better processes to make competing interests more visible and improve trade-offs. They cite the Ryfylke “seisaken” as an example where better evidence is needed to find workable solutions, but do not detail the conflict itself.
pq_notes.A7: The authors identify several industry-relevant actions and research directions that could improve spatial efficiency and sustainability. Larger and more exposed sites require technological innovation, and they call for a more professional innovation process with research conducted more often in established research infrastructure rather than operational production. They state that the industry itself is well placed to contribute to technology development and sterile-fish research, while other research needs may require action beyond the industry. They also describe Mainstream Norge’s willingness to delay stocking in inner Ofotfjorden and support a proposed ecological study as an example of industry cooperation. These are recommendations and a proposed case, not measured outcomes.

segments.summary:
This segment presents recommendations on coastal planning, property taxation and research needs for sustainable aquaculture. The authors propose regional and intermunicipal planning pilots in varied coastal areas, including places with growth potential, restructuring needs, local support and local opposition. They recommend state-sector participation, reports on knowledge gaps and planning methods, knowledge exchange, a project secretariat and local and regional co-financing. A state-funded project position is proposed for a three-year period. They also recommend a shared planning guide covering planning instruments, impact and risk assessments, building applications, relevant spatial data, other coastal interests and public participation.

The authors consider suitable sites scarce and explain that municipalities have been permitted since 1.1.2009 to levy property tax on floating marine aquaculture facilities. They report a tax of between ca. 25 000 and 70 000 kr per site per year and estimate hypothetical annual receipts of between 27 and 76 millioner kr for the 1093 salmon and trout sites present on 31. desember 2010, if all municipalities imposed the tax. They recommend evaluating the tax after production areas and release zones are established.

Research priorities include operational indicators for escaped fish and sea lice, effects on wild fish, regional environmental monitoring, and technology development. A proposed before-and-after study in inner Ofotfjorden would examine ecological effects through four work packages. Mainstream Norge planned two sites with ca. 1 million smolts at each and was willing to delay stocking until våren 2012; FHF was willing to consider co-funding the study for five–six years. The segment describes proposals and anticipated benefits, not completed evaluations or research findings.
